PREFACE 
The Seventy-seventh World Health Assembly was held at the Palais des Nations, Geneva, from  
27 May to 1 June 2024, in accordance with the decision of the Executive Board at its 153rd session.1

1 Decision EB153(10) (2023).

1. ADOPTION OF THE AGENDA AND ALLOCATION OF ITEMS TO THE MAIN 
COMMITTEES: (documents A77/1, A77/1 Add.1 and A77/GC/1) 
The CHAIR reminded the Committee that its terms of reference were set out in Rules 30 to 32 of 
the Rules of Procedure of the World Health Assembly. The provisional agenda was contained in 
document A77/1. The preliminary timetable was contained in document A77/GC/1. 
Proposed supplementary agenda item 
The CHAIR drew attention to a proposal, contained in document A77/1 Add.1, for the inclusion 
of a supplementary agenda item, “Inviting Taiwan to participate in the World Health Assembly as an 
observer”,1 on the provisional agenda of the Seventy-seventh World Health Assembly. The proposal 
had been received from 11 Member States. In line with the procedure followed in previous years, he 
suggested that two delegations should speak in favour of the proposal and two against, following which 
the recommendation not to include the supplementary agenda item would be made. 
It was so agreed. 
The representative of the MARSHALL ISLANDS2 said that the vision established in the WHO 
Constitution of the fundamental right of every human being to the enjoyment of the highest attainable 
standard of health should be upheld by recognizing the population of Taiwan3 and their right to 
participate in the global health security system, including through the participation of Taiwan in the 
Health Assembly as an observer, as had been the case between 2009 and 2016. Global health challenges 
made its participation more important than ever, as part of a more comprehensive global health 
framework to make the world healthier, more resilient and more equitable, and in keeping with the 
establishment in the WHO Constitution of the need for the fullest cooperation in the interests of global 
health. The coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic had shown that existing health coverage was 
inadequate; the exclusion of Taiwan impaired disease prevention efforts and jeopardized global health. 
As a responsible global health partner that had alerted WHO early on to cases of COVID-19 and had 
shared vital information on avian influenza, the inclusion of Taiwan would strengthen health emergency 
prevention, preparedness and response. Taiwan had also contributed to global health by improving

support the inclusion and participation of Taiwan in WHO meetings and activities. 
The representative of CHINA expressed his opposition to the inclusion of the proposed 
supplementary item relating to Taiwan on the agenda of the Health Assembly. The proposal lacked a 
legal basis, since the situation of Taiwan was a legacy of the Chinese Civil War and a domestic matter. 
The sovereignty and territory of China had never been divided and the legal status of Taiwan1 as part of 
that territory had not changed. United Nations General Assembly resolution 2758 (XXVI) (1971) and 
resolution WHA25.1 (1972) had resolved the issue of the representation of China, including Taiwan, at 
the United Nations and its specialized agencies, and set out the legal foundation for WHO to follow the 
one-China principle. United Nations documents had defined Taiwan as a province of China, which 
therefore could not participate in the Health Assembly without the consent of the Chinese central 
Government. Taiwan did not belong to any of the current categories of observers to the Health 
Assembly, which were sovereign States, state entities, international organizations and nongovernmental 
organizations. The separatist stance of the Taiwanese authorities had led to the disappearance of political 
space for the participation of Taiwan in the Health Assembly. More than 100 Member States had 
expressed their support for the position of China on the matter. The current proposal did not correspond 
to reality and speculated about the so-called gap in global anti-epidemic efforts; the Chinese central 
Government had approved the participation of Taiwan in WHO technical activities 21 times over the 
previous year, an IHR focal point based in Taiwan ensured prompt communication about health 
emergencies and there were diverse channels for the participation of Taiwan in WHO affairs. He called 
on the Committee to reject the proposal. 
The representative of SAINT LUCIA2 recalled that the WHO Constitution highlighted that the 
health of all peoples was fundamental to the attainment of peace and security and was dependent on the 
fullest cooperation of individuals and States – rendering essential the participation of all stakeholders in 
the Health Assembly, including that of Taiwan as an observer. The prolonged exclusion of Taiwan could 
impair disease prevention efforts and jeopardize global health, while WHO and the international 
community would greatly benefit from its inclusion as a willing and capable partner in a more resilient 
global health architecture and improved health emergency prevention, preparedness and response. 
Taiwan had shown its commitment to universal health coverage and to sharing experience and expertise 
by contributing to global efforts to realize the right to health for all, including by improving medical 
care in the South Pacific, bolstering climate change adaptability in the Caribbean, and supporting 
disaster relief efforts and providing humanitarian assistance in locations across the world. Taiwanese 
officials had reported that incomplete and delayed access to disease-related information had created a 
gap in domestic disease control and global disease prevention. The substantive engagement of Taiwan 
in international mechanisms relating to disease control and in the WHO Regional Office for the Western 
Pacific would enhance the global health system and the fight against communicable diseases. He called 
on the Committee to approve the proposal on the participation of Taiwan in the activities of the Health 
Assembly as an observer. 
The representative of CUBA said that there was only one China and the region of Taiwan was an 
integral and inalienable part of the territory of China. The participation of Taiwan in the work of 
international organizations, including WHO, must be in line with the one-China principle. United 
Nations General Assembly resolution 2758 (XXVI) and resolution WHA25.1 provided a solid legal 
basis for that approach, which was also applied to financial matters, such as the calculation of the 
assessments to the United Nations of the People’s Republic of China. The international community 
broadly supported the fair cause of the Government and people of China. The Government of the 
People’s Republic of China was the only legitimate representative of China, including Taiwan, and its

1. EXECUTIVE BOARD: ELECTION 
Proposals for the election of Members entitled to designate a person to serve on the 
Executive Board (document A77/GC/2) 
The CHAIR recalled that the procedure for drawing up the list of candidates to be transmitted by 
the General Committee to the Health Assembly for the purpose of the annual election of Members 
entitled to designate a person to serve on the Executive Board was governed by Article 24 of the WHO 
Constitution and Rule 101 of the Rules of Procedure of the World Health Assembly. In accordance with 
those provisions, the Committee needed to nominate 12 new Members for that purpose. 
Two documents had been prepared to assist the Committee in its task. The first indicated the 
present composition of the Executive Board by region; the names of the 12 Members whose term of 
office would expire at the end of the Seventy-seventh World Health Assembly and who had to be 
replaced were underlined. The second (document A77/GC/2) contained a list of the 12 Members that it 
was suggested should be entitled to designate a person to serve on the Executive Board. Vacancies by 
region were: African Region: 1; Region of the Americas: 2; Eastern Mediterranean Region: 2; European 
Region: 4; South-East Asia Region: 1; and Western Pacific Region: 2.  
As no additional suggestions had been made by the Committee, the number of candidates was 
equal to the number of vacant seats on the Executive Board. He therefore took it that the Committee 
wished, in accordance with Rule 80 of the Rules of Procedure, to proceed without taking a ballot. 
There being no objection, he concluded that it was the Committee’s wish, in accordance with 
Rule 102 of the Rules of Procedure, to transmit to the Health Assembly the following list of 
12 candidates for the annual election of Members entitled to designate a person to serve on the Executive 
Board: Bulgaria, Brunei Darussalam, Chile, Costa Rica, Israel, Lebanon, Norway, Poland, Republic of 
Korea, Somalia, Thailand and Zimbabwe.  
It was so agreed.

2. DRAFT FOURTEENTH GENERAL PROGRAMME OF WORK, 2025–2028: Item 17 of 
the agenda (documents A77/16 and A77/34) 
The CHAIR drew the Committee’s attention to the draft resolution contained in document 
A77/16. 
The CHAIR OF THE PROGRAMME, BUDGET AND ADMINISTRATION COMMITTEE 
welcomed the consultative approach to the development of the draft fourteenth general programme of 
work, 2025–2028, and expressed support for its overarching goal and strategic objectives, which would 
provide continuity with the Thirteenth General Programme of Work, 2019–2025. The Programme, 
Budget and Administration Committee had welcomed the emphasis on WHO’s comparative strengths, 
its unique added value and its normative and leadership roles in the global health ecosystem, as reflected 
in the cross-cutting corporate outcomes. To that end, the sustainable financing of the Organization was 
vital, and he emphasized the importance of the forthcoming investment round and of ensuring adequate 
human resources. He encouraged the Secretariat to continue developing the results framework for the 
draft fourteenth general programme of work, to ensure alignment across the different levels of the results 
chain; and to continue to engage with Member States in the development of the draft Proposed 
programme budget 2026–2027. He urged the Committee to approve the draft resolution.  
The representative of BELGIUM, speaking on behalf of the European Union and its Member 
States, said that the candidate countries North Macedonia, Montenegro, Serbia, Albania, Ukraine, the 
Republic of Moldova, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Georgia, as well as the EFTA country Iceland, 
member of the European Economic Area, aligned themselves with his statement. He welcomed 
the inclusive approach taken to the development of the draft fourteenth general programme of work, 
2025–2028, and its focus on WHO’s comparative strengths. WHO, its unique contribution to global 
health and its standard-setting function must be preserved. Noting the interrelated factors that had 
influenced its development, he welcomed the overarching goal of the draft fourteenth general 
programme of work and its six strategic objectives and encouraged WHO to maintain its focus on a 
human rights-based approach to sexual and reproductive health. He emphasized the importance of 
WHO’s evidence-based guidelines, which enabled Member States to address mis- and disinformation. 
He welcomed the plans to develop the health workforce to improve health services. Recognizing the 
value of the Health in All Policies and One Health approaches, he expressed support for WHO’s global 
health leadership and collaboration with all relevant actors. WHO must be equipped to face the changing 
world, and strengthening national and regional capacities should be a priority. It would be important to 
ensure adequate, sustainable and predictable funding for the programme budget for the duration of the 
fourteenth general programme of work, including through the planned investment round. 
The representative of EGYPT, speaking on behalf of the Member States of the Eastern 
Mediterranean Region, commended the consultative process that had led to the development of the draft 
fourteenth general programme of work, 2025–2028. He welcomed the inclusion of recommendations 
from the evaluation of the Thirteenth General Programme of Work, 2019–2025, and proposed that the 
Secretariat should carry out a regular evaluation of the fourteenth general programme of work, with a 
focus on the impact on people’s health. While he appreciated the ambitious targets of the draft fourteenth 
general programme of work, which would accelerate efforts towards the attainment of the health-related 
Sustainable Develop Goals, achieving those targets would require significant political commitment, 
leadership and action beyond the health sector.  
The Secretariat should seek to reduce the reporting burden on Member States by aligning the draft 
fourteenth general programme of work with country priorities and WHO’s existing results framework. 
Using health information systems effectively would enable progress to be measured and ensure that 
policies had the greatest impact. He noted efforts to address data gaps and called on the Secretariat to

The CO-CHAIRS OF THE WORKING GROUP ON AMENDMENTS TO THE 
INTERNATIONAL HEALTH REGULATIONS (2005), speaking in turn to present the results of the 
Working Group, said that, since November 2022, more than 300 proposed amendments to the 
International Health Regulations (2005) submitted by States Parties had been carefully considered, 
discussed and refined. The recommendations of the Review Committee regarding amendments to the 
International Health Regulations (2005) had provided a solid basis for the work of the Working Group; 
the Committee’s final report and the interest and contributions from civil society organization had also 
proved invaluable. Applauding participants’ extraordinary commitment and outstanding spirit of 
negotiation during the Working Group’s numerous meetings, they expressed appreciation for the trust 
placed in the Bureau of the Working Group and for the Secretariat’s excellent advice and active support. 
Every effort had been made to develop a package of targeted amendments designed to strengthen 
and update the Regulations. Importantly, throughout the process, there had been an unwavering and 
universal commitment to incorporating equity-related provisions. The Working Group was very close 
to producing an agreed package of amendments. Some of the historic amendments proposed had already 
been agreed, and there was momentum and an aspiration among participants to complete the task.  
Finalizing and adopting a package of amendments that would make the Regulations fairer, more 
exhaustive and equitable would be a significant achievement, and would constitute a stepping stone 
towards the successful conclusion of the negotiations on a pandemic agreement. The Working Group 
stood ready to continue discussions in the coming days, so that the amendments could be adopted by the 
Seventy-seventh World Health Assembly.

Mediterranean Region, said that the Region, which continued to face escalating emergencies, recognized 
the importance of the International Health Regulations (2005) in preventing and responding to health 
threats and mitigating the spread of diseases. The decision by Member States, following the COVID-19 
pandemic, to explore potential targeted amendments to the Regulations to enhance their effectiveness, 
promote compliance and address gaps demonstrated their collective commitment to strengthening global 
health security. Noting that equity, solidarity, international cooperation, trust-building, transparency and 
sovereignty had been cross-cutting themes in the amendment process, he said that the proposed 
amendments should enhance Member States’ capacities relating to health emergency and pandemic

workforce. Member States of the Region appreciated the leadership of Saudi Arabia in the Working

The representative of BELGIUM, speaking on behalf of the European Union and its Member 
States, said that the candidate countries North Macedonia, Montenegro, Serbia, Ukraine, and Bosnia and 
Herzegovina aligned themselves with the statement. An emphasis should be placed on two core aspects 
of universal health coverage, namely improving access to quality health services to advance health 
outcomes and reduce health inequalities, and providing financial protection to reduce financial hardship, 
especially for those with lower incomes. Developing primary health care had been proven to accelerate 
the achievement of comprehensive, effective and equitable universal health coverage. That required 
sustainable investment in education, training and remuneration for the health workforce. To create 
 COMMITTEE A: FIFTH MEETING 79 
 
 
 
 
inclusive, integrated and person-centred health systems, it was critical to strengthen integrated and 
community-oriented primary health care, social prescribing and public health services, while ensuring 
equitable and affordable access to essential health services, especially for people in vulnerable and 
marginalized situations. It was also crucial to apply a gender-responsive approach to policy development 
and implementation. Expressing support for the Beijing Platform for Action and the Programme of 
Action of the International Conference on Population and Development, he reaffirmed that access to 
comprehensive, high-quality and affordable sexual and reproductive health information, education and 
care services was fundamental to universal health coverage.  
A strong and accessible primary health care sector was also key to accommodating the health care 
needs associated with noncommunicable diseases and mental illness, and to addressing the growing 
challenges arising from comorbidity, ageing populations and climate change. Increased investment in 
research was needed to establish innovative approaches to structural health promotion and disease 
prevention, especially in the primary health care setting. The economic, commercial, social and 
environmental root causes of noncommunicable diseases and mental health conditions should be 
addressed through a Health in All Policies and whole-of-society approach. The Member States of the 
European Union wished to be added to the list of sponsors of the draft resolution on strengthening mental 
health and psychosocial support before, during and after armed conflicts, natural and human-caused 
disasters and health and other emergencies. 
The representative of LEBANON, speaking on behalf of the Member States of the Eastern 
Mediterranean Region, welcomed the advancements made towards the target of one billion more people 
enjoying better health and well-being, which demonstrated the importance of investing in prevention. 
However, it was disappointing that progress towards the other triple billion targets had stagnated. 
Drawing attention to the financial hardship faced by many people in the Region, especially in fragile, 
conflict-affected areas, she stressed the need to enhance the resilience of health systems to improve both 
universal health coverage and health security. To that end, the Regional Director was leading three 
flagship initiatives focused on control of substance use, investing in a resilient health workforce and 
securing equitable access to quality medical products and supply chains.  
She welcomed the proposal to develop a global strategy and action plan for integrated emergency, 
critical and operative care, given the need to strengthen such provision as part of essential health 
services. She also commended efforts to monitor progress on noncommunicable diseases. However, it 
was concerning that the international community was not on course to achieve target 3.4 of the 
Sustainable Development Goals. Regional efforts would continue to reduce risk factors for 
noncommunicable diseases, including by integrating monitoring services into primary health care. A 
new regional action plan was also being developed on mental health and psychosocial support in 
emergencies. 
The representative of ETHIOPIA, speaking on behalf of the Member States of the African Region, 
said there was an urgent need to close gaps in universal health coverage in terms of access, quality and 
affordability, especially in low-resource and fragile health systems. Despite efforts to mitigate 
disruptions caused by crises such as the coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic, climate change and 
economic recessions, access to essential services remained relatively poor in the Region, due to 
inadequate investment, particularly from domestic resources, leading to financial hardship for 
individuals. There was also a rising burden of noncommunicable diseases, mental health conditions and 
oral diseases, with key challenges including a lack of prioritization, shortages in human resources, 
limited interventions at the primary and community levels, insufficient laboratory resources, and weak 
surveillance and monitoring systems. 
To address those issues, he agreed that health systems must be reoriented towards an integrated, 
person-centred primary health care approach with a view to providing high-quality and affordable 
universal health coverage that was sustainably financed through both domestic and external sources. 
That required strong political commitment and leadership at the country level. It was likewise important 
to strengthen capacities for public health expertise, surveillance and monitoring, and to promote 
evidence-based policy-making for noncommunicable diseases and mental health. He further called for

the development of comprehensive, integrated noncommunicable disease and mental health service

capacities must also be developed, and further work undertaken to improve the availability, affordability

The representative of THAILAND, speaking on behalf of the Member States of the South-East 
Asia Region, said that e-cigarettes, ambient air pollution and mental health disorders and comorbidities 
were critical threats linked to noncommunicable diseases. Member States should strengthen and enforce 
legal and regulatory measures controlling the use and marketing of e-cigarettes, address cross-border 
trafficking of tobacco products and e-cigarettes, and enhance public awareness of the problems 
associated with their use. Tackling transboundary air pollution required collective efforts and political 
commitment, including strict enforcement of environmental regulations and implementation of 
monitoring systems. Interventions to address the rising burden of mental health disorders, especially 
among adolescents, should focus on reducing social anxiety and stigma; developing promotion and 
prevention measures; and strengthening early detection and treatment. Community-based mental health 
services should also be prioritized. 
To overcome challenges related to universal health coverage, Member States must integrate health 
promotion and disease prevention – at both the individual and population levels – into universal health 
coverage benefit packages. Individuals should be empowered to improve their own health through 
greater health literacy, which had proven crucial for health system resilience during pandemics. It was 
also important to foster social participation by involving communities in policy-making, policy 
implementation and resource mobilization, as universal health coverage could only be achieved with the 
involvement of multiple stakeholders, including those outside the health sector. He therefore supported 
the draft resolution on social participation for universal health coverage, health and well-being. 
The representative of NORWAY, speaking on behalf of the Nordic and Baltic countries, said that 
social participation based on equality, mutual respect, inclusiveness and transparency was key to 
ensuring progress towards universal health coverage. She therefore welcomed the draft resolution on 
the subject. Adequate public spending on health was also essential to ensure a sufficient and 
appropriately skilled workforce, promote access to essential medicines, and strengthen prevention and 
primary health care services for both physical and mental health. Global health initiatives and 
international financing must be coordinated and managed on the basis of strict accountability to support 
countries on their path to universal health coverage. To that end, she welcomed the conclusions of the 
Future of Global Health Initiatives process (Lusaka Agenda) and the support provided by the Secretariat 
and other stakeholders for country-led health systems strengthening. She underscored that universal 
access to sexual and reproductive health services was an integral part of universal health coverage and 
a right in itself.

health conditions, she called for the full integration of related services into primary health care and the 
strengthening of health promotion and prevention activities through intersectoral collaboration. The lack

of the General Assembly on the prevention and control of non-communicable diseases in 2025; those 
preparations should also reflect the importance of structural measures such as regulation and taxation, 
and of primary health care, particularly for rural and poorer populations. Changing individual health

strengthening mental health and psychosocial support, stressing the importance of responding to the 
unmet needs of those affected by armed conflict and humanitarian crises, especially women and girls,

and health promotion with communities and to engage young people as health volunteers and leaders in 
tuberculosis interventions. 
The representative of PUBLIC SERVICES INTERNATIONAL, speaking at the invitation of the 
CHAIR, urged Member States to allocate funding to ensure clean water and sanitary conditions in health 
facilities and to support low- and middle-income countries in building capacity for disease surveillance 
and maintaining public health standards. Noting that health workers had called for the precautionary 
principle to be applied in the implementation of infection prevention and control guidelines during the 
COVID-19 pandemic, he encouraged Member States to apply that principle to protect the lives of health 
workers. He urged Member States to invest in and support health workers, with a view to restoring 
essential immunization activities, and called on Member States to develop policies to ensure health 
workers’ safety and health, reduce occupational risks and provide appropriate insurance and 
compensation. 
The representative of MOVENDI INTERNATIONAL, speaking at the invitation of the CHAIR, 
highlighted the need to integrate treatment of alcohol use disorders with tuberculosis prevention and 
care. Globally, 400 million adults had an alcohol use disorder, meaning that millions of people were at 
high risk of tuberculosis, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. She called on WHO and 
Member States to make full use of population-level alcohol policy solutions to lower the tuberculosis 
burden. Alcohol taxation was essential to preventing and reducing tuberculosis cases and helped 
countries to raise domestic resources while reducing the prevalence of alcohol as a tuberculosis risk 
factor.  
A representative of the REGIONAL DIRECTOR FOR THE AMERICAS said that, globally, 
tuberculosis was the leading cause of death from infectious diseases. According to the WHO Global 
Tuberculosis Report 2023, an estimated 10.6 million cases had been reported globally, with 1.3 million 
120 SEVENTY-SEVENTH WORLD HEALTH ASSEMBLY 
 
 
 
 
deaths. Global efforts to combat tuberculosis had saved some 75 million lives since 2000. The impact 
of the COVID-19 pandemic continued to be felt in the implementation of tuberculosis programmes, and 
trends in case notifications varied among regions. Member States were making significant efforts to 
reverse upwards trends in tuberculosis incidence and mortality. It would be necessary to increase 
investment, strengthen multisectoral collaboration and ensure the adoption of the latest WHO 
recommendations.  
AMRO/PAHO was working with its Member States to place equity at the heart of the tuberculosis 
response and accelerate the implementation of innovative technologies, with a focus on strengthening 
primary health care. The PAHO Elimination Initiative provided an opportunity to address those 
challenges through efforts aimed at increasing equitable access to quality health services, building 
resilient health systems through community- and people-centred approaches and addressing social and 
environmental determinants of health to reach populations in situations of vulnerability. Measures taken 
at the national level included the establishment in 2023 by the Government of Brazil of an 
interministerial committee for the elimination of tuberculosis and other socially determined diseases and 
the development in 2024, by the Government of Colombia of a national disease elimination plan. In 
2022, 14 countries and territories in the Region of the Americas had achieved low tuberculosis 
incidence, and some were now close to elimination thresholds. The Region was in a unique position to 
eliminate tuberculosis by 2030, and could spearhead global efforts in that regard. 
The ASSISTANT DIRECTOR-GENERAL (Universal Health Coverage/Life Course) noted with 
appreciation the support demonstrated by Member States for the draft global action plan and monitoring 
framework on infection prevention and control. Recognizing that the availability of resources posed a 
challenge to implementation, the Secretariat would shortly hold consultations with Member States to 
seek options for mobilizing resources in addition to domestic resources and was working with OECD to 
build a business case in that regard. In response to comments made by Member States, he noted that the 
supplementary annexes to the draft global action plan contained information on global collaboration and 
the role of WHO, and that the issue of air quality had been captured in key action 2 of strategic 
direction 2 of the draft global action plan.  
Despite setbacks resulting from the COVID-19 pandemic, progress was being made towards the 
goals of the Immunization Agenda 2030, including through the Big Catch-Up. It was now important to 
move beyond the recovery stage and get back on track to achieve the goals of the Immunization Agenda 
2030, in particular by reaching zero-dose children. Immunization Agenda 2030 partners had established 
a team to support Member States in outbreak response. He welcomed the steps taken by Member States 
to address gaps in measles immunization coverage and increase uptake of human papillomavirus 
vaccine, highlighting the important role of Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, in those efforts. In the 50 years 
since the launch of the Expanded Programme on Immunization, over 150 million lives had been saved; 
to save even more, it was clear that immunization should be integrated into work on primary health care 
systems. The Secretariat would consult with Member States in early 2025 on accelerating work on the 
development of the tuberculosis vaccine. 
The ASSISTANT DIRECTOR-GENERAL (Universal Health Coverage/Communicable 
Diseases and Noncommunicable Diseases) said that the End TB Strategy had been instrumental in 
guiding global efforts to end tuberculosis. Since 2015, 80 countries had reduced incidence by more than 
20% and 45 countries had reduced mortality by more than 35%. In 2023, 8 million people had received 
access to treatment, the highest number since 1995. However, only 70% of people with tuberculosis and 
49% of children with the disease had gained access to treatment in 2022, and drug resistance continued 
to pose a major threat.  
To end the epidemic by 2030, it would be crucial to expand services, establish supportive policies 
and systems and vigorously pursue research and innovation, with a view to developing and applying 
new tools. More diagnostic tests and safer, shorter-term oral treatment had become available, 
significantly improving patient outcomes. However, funding remained critical to ensuring that everyone 
could receive the care that they needed. He took note of the importance placed by Member States on 
fostering high-level collaboration and accountability to address key drivers of tuberculosis; ensuring

and technical assistance.

The representative of BELGIUM, speaking on behalf of the European Union and its Member 
States, said that the Member States of the European Union wished to be added to the list of sponsors of 
the draft resolution on accelerating progress towards reducing maternal, newborn and child mortality in 
order to achieve Sustainable Development Goal targets 3.1 and 3.2.  
Welcoming the inclusion of antimicrobial resistance on the agenda, she said that the candidate 
countries Türkiye, North Macedonia, Montenegro, Serbia, Albania, Ukraine, the Republic of Moldova, 
Bosnia and Herzegovina and Georgia, the EFTA countries Iceland and Norway, members of the 
European Economic Area, as well as Armenia, aligned themselves with her statement. Antimicrobial 
resistance was driven by a lack of regulation and guidance on the use of antimicrobial agents, and climate 
change and humanitarian crises, and was exacerbated by inequality. Responsible use of antimicrobial 
agents and high standards of surveillance, prevention and control were key. Evidence-based WHO 
guidance was welcome, since tackling antimicrobial resistance required the availability of, and access 
to, safe and effective antimicrobial agents, vaccines and diagnostics. She encouraged support for 
research and development and access to new and existing antimicrobial agents and other medical 
technologies, through collaboration with academic institutions, civil society organizations and the 
private sector. The Secretariat should develop more evidence-based and cost-effective policy measures 
to ensure prudent use of antimicrobial agents; existing measures were too focused on passive strategies 
that were insufficient to achieve the necessary targets. More emphasis was needed on structural and 
prescriptive measures. Negotiations on a high-level political declaration on antimicrobial resistance 
must be accompanied by strong political commitment; she called for the setting of tangible objectives 
and measurable targets, as well as measures to integrate the One Health approach at all levels.  
A whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach was essential, as were efforts to ensure 
sufficient and sustainable funding. She called on the Secretariat to continue its strong collaboration with 
other quadripartite organizations. 
The representative of SOMALIA, speaking on behalf of the Member States of the Eastern 
Mediterranean Region, said that a number of countries in the Region were not on track to meet the 2030 
maternal health and child mortality targets, while others were struggling to sustain previous gains. 
Despite multistakeholder efforts to scale up evidence-based interventions and integrated strategies, and 
implement global and regional initiatives, additional action was needed to accelerate progress. The 
Member States of the Eastern Mediterranean Region supported the draft resolution on reducing 
maternal, newborn and child mortality and called for continued commitment to, investment in, and 
cooperation on maternal and child health. Further efforts were required to combat antimicrobial 
resistance: the Region had the highest – and rapidly rising – rates of antimicrobial consumption and 
higher-than-average antimicrobial resistance rates, which were also increasing. Following the 
establishment in several countries of frameworks to tackle antimicrobial resistance and strengthen 
infection prevention and control, there was a need to implement WHO strategies and priorities, and to 
adopt a people-centred approach as a basis for the regional approach to building resilient health systems. 
Encouraging progress had been made in the Region on neglected tropical diseases, including the 
elimination in eight countries of at least one disease and a significant reduction in the number of people 
who required interventions for neglected tropical diseases between 2010 and 2021. More work was 
needed, however, particularly to tackle leishmaniasis and mycetoma, and overcome challenges relating 
to population movement and climate change. He encouraged further action, guided by the road map for 
neglected tropical diseases, 2021–2030. 
The representative of the UNITED REPUBLIC OF TANZANIA, speaking on behalf of the 
Member States of the African Region, noted that efforts on neglected tropical diseases had allowed 
19 countries in the Region to eliminate at least one disease, and welcomed the inclusion of noma disease 
on the list of neglected tropical diseases. As the coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic receded, 
however, additional resources and unearmarked funding were needed to consistently address neglected 
tropical diseases, particularly in the African Region, and support the Secretariat’s work in that area. 
Given that many countries in the Region were not set to meet the 2030 targets for maternal health and 
child mortality, radical measures were needed to reorient primary health care and strengthen the

implementation of proven interventions. Universal access to quality, comprehensive reproductive, 
maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health services was essential, including through investment in 
nutrition and measures to promote and protect health. Progress had been made in the Region on 
antimicrobial resistance, including through the development of national action plans, yet there was 
insufficient financing for their implementation. Support from WHO and partners was needed to support 
the Global Antimicrobial Resistance and Use Surveillance System. 
The representative of BANGLADESH, speaking on behalf of the Member States of the 
South-East Asia Region, stressed the serious burden posed by antimicrobial resistance, which impeded 
efforts to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals. Antimicrobial resistance was a priority for the 
Region and he supported negotiations towards a high-level political declaration on the subject. Progress 
was slow, with the implementation of national action plans hampered by limited funding. Greater efforts 
were needed on areas including infection prevention and control, surveillance of antimicrobial resistance 
and consumption, and regulation of self-medicated antibiotic use. A One Health approach was essential, 
given the interconnected nature of human, animal and environmental health ecosystems, alongside 
multisectoral action to address the root causes of antimicrobial resistance across all sectors. In particular, 
the environmental sector in several countries in the Region lacked control mechanisms. The Member 
States of the Region endorsed the draft resolution on antimicrobial resistance and were committed to 
engaging in the work of the high-level meeting of the General Assembly on antimicrobial resistance 
later in 2024. 
The representative of DENMARK, speaking on behalf of the Nordic and Baltic countries, 
welcomed the draft resolution on antimicrobial resistance. Cooperation on antimicrobial resistance was 
needed at all levels. Many regions faced stock shortages and problems in ensuring access to antibiotics; 
countries in the Region were cooperating to ensure sustainable production of narrow spectrum 
antibiotics, including through joint procurement and the development of financial models. The 
Secretariat should support cooperation to accelerate measures to tackle antimicrobial resistance, 
including through infection prevention, access to quality diagnostics and medicines, and a 
people-centred approach. The high-level meeting of the General Assembly on antimicrobial resistance 
was a unique opportunity to mount a global response based on a One Health approach. Cross-cutting 
public health measures were needed, including on immunization and maternal and child health.  
Global maternal mortality rates had stagnated or increased, with most deaths involving 
preventable causes. There was a need for equitable access to sexual and reproductive health services, 
including access to contraception, free and safe abortion, and comprehensive sexuality education. The 
Organization had a crucial role to play in supporting Member States’ efforts to meet ambitious 
objectives, challenge existing standards and focus on evidence-based, technical guidelines. The 
Secretariat was urged to support Member States in ensuring women’s and children’s health, in particular 
their sexual and reproductive health and rights. 
The representative of SAMOA said that antimicrobial resistance posed a particular challenge for 
Pacific island States, where resistant infections were on the rise in a context of constraints, such as poor 
availability of medicines, laboratory capacity and trained personnel. Antimicrobial resistance was 
exacerbating the vulnerability of health systems in small island developing States that were already 
under pressure due to climate change. Cross-sectoral action was needed to tackle the problem, including 
its social and economic dimensions, and the associated clinical, scientific and operational challenges. 
He expressed appreciation for the global action plan on antimicrobial resistance and the Framework for 
Accelerating Action to Fight Antimicrobial Resistance in the Western Pacific Region. The measures 
taken by his Government included the adoption of a national action plan on antimicrobial resistance. He 
called for financial and technical support, including with regard to surveillance, infection prevention 
and control, stewardship programmes and supply chain management.

and viral hepatitis acquisition rates. Member States must prioritize an integrated, person-centred 
approach to the prevention and treatment of HIV, co-infections and comorbidities. Donors and other key 
actors must continue to invest in and prioritize the health of those most affected by HIV, viral hepatitis 
and sexually transmitted diseases. 
The representative of the DRUGS FOR NEGLECTED DISEASES INITIATIVE, speaking at the 
invitation of the CHAIR, urged Member States to support the development, introduction and scaling up 
of appropriate treatment options, including paediatric formulations, to improve health outcomes for 
people with advanced HIV, who were also highly susceptible to cryptococcal meningitis. While 
treatments for that disease existed, they were often difficult to administer and access to them was limited.

including patent barriers, and include new, affordable, direct-acting antiviral medicines in national 
essential medicines lists.  
The representative of the INTERNATIONAL PLANNED PARENTHOOD FEDERATION, 
speaking at the invitation of the CHAIR, regretted the slow progress in reducing deaths related to 
congenital syphilis and cervical cancer, both of which were easily preventable. People-centred care for

health care. Her organization was alarmed that attacks on reproductive health and rights were obstructing

efforts to eliminate those diseases. Information about condoms and other protective measures was not 
universally available, and threats to gender rights further marginalized key communities. Those issues 
must be more adequately addressed when implementing the draft fourteenth general programme of 
work, 2025–2028. 
The ASSISTANT DIRECTOR-GENERAL (Universal Health Coverage/Life Course), 
responding on behalf of his Assistant Director-General colleagues, noted in particular the emphasis on, 
and concern regarding, implementation of the global health sector strategies on, respectively, HIV, viral 
hepatitis and sexually transmitted infections, for the period 2022–2030; the guidance and advice on 
universal health coverage; the focus on advancing the reproductive health strategy; and the specific 
advice on people-centred eye care, transplantation, pandemic prevention, the public health dimensions 
of the world drug problem and food safety. The Secretariat shared the concern that a substantial number 
of countries were yet to fully integrate gender analysis and had, following discussions with Member 
States and partner agencies, included that topic in the draft fourteenth general programme of work, 
2025–2028, to ensure that gender was recognized as a key determinant for achieving universal health 
coverage and that the Secretariat enacted the analytics and steps necessary. He confirmed that the overall

gender-disaggregated data even at the country level. The Secretariat was committed to providing 
additional training in that area through the WHO Academy and under the draft fourteenth general 
programme of work. 
The ASSISTANT DIRECTOR-GENERAL (Access to Medicines and Health Products) 
(Antimicrobial Resistance ad interim) thanked Member States for highlighting the importance of access 
to quality-assured, safe, effective and affordable health products in order to achieve universal health 
coverage and other Sustainable Development Goals, as well as the need for access to controlled 
medicines, such as narcotic drugs for pain control, which was complicated by the need to avoid their 
harmful use. The Secretariat had been working closely with UNODC to ensure access to medicines 
subject to international drug control treaties, and had published a report in 2023 on the disparity in 
morphine access and ways to improve access and affordability. Comprehensive recommendations would 
be issued later in the year 2024 on policy initiatives that countries could take to ensure balanced, 
equitable and safe access to controlled medicines. The Secretariat would also update the road map for 
access to medicines, vaccines and other health products 2019–2023, and hold consultations with 
Member States in that regard in 2024.

The Seventy-seventh World Health Assembly, 
(PP1) Having considered the consolidated report by the Director-General;2 
(PP2) Recalling the Constitution of the World Health Organization, which recognizes that 
health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of 
disease or infirmity, and that the enjoyment of the highest attainable standard of health is one of 
the fundamental rights of every human being without distinction of race, religion, political belief, 
economic or social condition;  
(PP3) Recalling also United Nations General Assembly resolution 70/1 (2015) and the 
commitments made to achieving sustainable development in its three dimensions – economic, 
social and environmental – in a balanced and integrated manner through the 2030 Agenda for 
Sustainable Development, in particular Goal 3 (Ensure healthy lives and promote well-being for 
all at all ages), including indicator 3.8.2 (Proportion of population with large household 
expenditures on health as a share of total household expenditure or income), as well as the pledge 
to leave no one behind;

(PP7) Noting resolutions WHA58.33 (2005) on sustainable health financing, universal

financing structures and universal coverage, WHA72.8 (2019) on improving the transparency of

preparedness for health emergencies: implementation of the International Health Regulations

technologies to improve access, WHA74.16 (2021) on social determinants of health and 
WHA75.19 (2022) on well-being and health promotion;  
(PP8) Recalling the Declaration of Alma-Ata (1978) and noting the work done within 
WHO at global and regional levels on the linkage between the economy, health and well-being, 
including the Geneva Charter for Well-being (2021);  
(PP9) Recognizing that economic policies need to be fiscally sustainable, socially 
responsible and inclusive, and recognizing the need to consider environmental health in economic 
policy-making, as well as the role of equity, gender equality, solidarity, cohesion and 
sustainability for all in mainstream economic analysis, modelling and evaluation;  
(PP10) Recognizing also that health and the economy are interconnected, and that in this 
regard, an economy of well-being perspective can be used to put people and their health and 
well-being at the centre of decision-making, underlining the mutually reinforcing nature of health, 
well-being and the economy;  
(PP11) Recognizing further that a sound and sustainable economic policy highlights the 
importance of investing in effective, efficient and equitable measures and structures, including 
health system infrastructure, that ensure equal access for all, particularly women and girls, to 
public services, including health services, with a particular focus on equitable access to primary 
health care, health promotion and disease prevention, as well as social services and long-term 
care, while providing protection against financial risks;  
(PP12) Also recognizing that efficient, long-term investments in the determinants of health 
and well-being can contribute to curbing the rise in health and social welfare costs, and are 
therefore an investment in future generations;  
(PP13) Further recognizing that the coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic and other 
crises and their direct and indirect impacts, as well as major developments such as digitalization, 
demographic change and macroeconomic constraints underline the critical importance of 
investments in health systems, including in the health workforce and in tackling broader 
determinants of health, including social exclusion factors, malnutrition, poor housing and bad 
working conditions, lack of access to education and other entrenched inequities, and that these 
investments are critical for pandemic prevention, preparedness and response and for resilient 
societies, communities and economies;

(PP14) Recognizing also that insufficient health expenditure significantly undermines 
population health outcomes by restricting access to health services, hampering the development 
of health infrastructure, contributing to shortages of skilled health professionals, limiting 
preventive measures, increasing the burden of both communicable and noncommunicable 
diseases, reducing the capacity for emergency response and exacerbating health inequalities, 
leaving those in vulnerable situations at a greater disadvantage, while also noting with concern 
the negative impact of economic constraints in some countries that undermine their ability to 
invest in the health sector; 
(PP15) Recognizing further that while the enjoyment of the highest attainable standard of 
health is one of the fundamental rights of every human being, the progressive realization of that 
right requires commitment to long-term comprehensive, equitable and sustainable investment that 
matters for health and well-being for all;  
(PP16) Also recognizing that the enjoyment of the highest attainable standard of physical 
and mental health throughout the life course of all women and girls, the achievement of gender 
equality, and the recognition of the value of unpaid care and domestic work and the roles of 
women in constituting the majority of the health workforce globally are crucial for sustainable, 
equitable and inclusive economies, development and well-being for all; 
(PP17) Acknowledging that health for all is not just the concern of health ministries but is 
relevant across the whole of government and whole of society and from the perspective of a Health 
in All Policies approach, requiring policy coherence and accountability across sectors, to shape 
and redesign public policies, partnerships, institutions and tools for common goods for health, 
while advancing gender mainstreaming and leaving no one behind;  
(PP18) Recognizing the need to increase the engagement of nongovernmental actors, 
including the private sector, in contributing to equitable health and well-being, as well as the 
critical role of the government in ensuring stewardship and providing for access to equitable 
health services for all and accountability, while acknowledging different national contexts; 
(PP19) Recognizing also the importance of the health of people and the environment as a 
foundation for prosperous economies and societies, as well as the need for a holistic approach 
when making decisions regarding the well-being of people, and therefore the importance of 
engaging with civil society and local communities, ensuring diversity and inclusion in designing 
and implementing policies that recognize the interlinkage between well-being, health and the 
economy;  
(PP20) Recognizing further the critical role of WHO in strengthening leadership for health 
and well-being in national and international development policies to prevent and mitigate social, 
environmental, economic and other risks to health, and underlining the importance of WHO 
showing leadership on advocating for financing for health and well-being across sectors as the 
United Nations agency that acts as the directing and coordinating authority on international health; 
(PP21) Taking note of the work done on the interlinkage between well-being, health and 
the economy by the United Nations, its specialized agencies and relevant international 
organizations, such as the World Bank Group, International Monetary Fund, International Labour 
Organization and Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, among others, and 
the strengthening of dialogue between health and finance sectors towards sustainable financing 
of health,  
(OP)1. URGES Member States1 in accordance with national context and priorities:  
(1) to consider the interlinkage between health and the economy and include an 
economy of well-being perspective horizontally into national policies and put people and 
their health and well-being at the centre of policy-making; 
(2) to implement, where appropriate, evidence-based and effective policy interventions 
at national level that reorient economic and innovation strategies towards health and 
well-being for all, including consideration for the needs of those in vulnerable situations;

(3) to invest in health system infrastructure, including capacitating and retaining human 
resources for health, in order to deliver on essential public health functions and access to 
quality health services, including through domestic financing and official development 
assistance based on needs for achievement of universal health coverage; 
(4) to work towards shifting public and private investments from activities that are 
harmful for people’s health and well-being towards investments that improve them, 
including through enhancing corporate social responsibility; 
(5) to consider the mutually reinforcing linkages between the economy and the health of 
humans, animals, plants and the environment, critical to the resilience and stability of 
economies worldwide, requiring multisectoral and cost-effective actions and the prevention 
of drivers of biodiversity loss, pollution and climate change;  
(6) to address social and economic determinants that result in health inequities, 
including gender inequalities and differences in the level of development, and that 
disproportionately affect those in vulnerable and marginalized situations and hard-to-reach 
populations, and shape their unequal distribution within and across countries, while leaving 
no one behind; 
(7) to recognize that health is a prerequisite for development and that as part of broader 
sustainable development strategies, policies need to actively pursue in a mutually 
reinforcing manner inclusive economic development and healthy populations, as well as 
sustainable societies, including resilient health systems, with a view to a balance of 
short-term and long-term multisectoral investments that enable sustained health and  
well-being over time and for future generations; 
(8) to recognize the importance of putting in place multisectoral capacities and 
mechanisms at the national level to reorient the economy that characterize financing for 
health as an investment rather than as an expenditure, calling for shifts, including equipping 
and enabling engagement between all relevant sectors including the health and financial 
sectors and drawing from the evidence base on the linkage between health and the economy 
and the importance of mobilizing domestic financing, and the potential role of innovative 
and complementary financing in this regard; 
(OP)2. ENCOURAGES Member States, international and regional financial institutions and other 
international, regional and national partners, nongovernmental stakeholders, donors and partners 
consistent with their respective mandates: 
(1) to support, together with the Secretariat, the balance between economic, social and 
environmental dimensions in decision-making, including by creating opportunities for 
dialogue between the public finance and health sectors, including engaging regional 
economic associations and international finance institutions, and national and regional 
development banks to consider in their agenda, as appropriate, the economics of health for 
all as well as the cost–effectiveness and fiscal sustainability of health systems; 
(2) to support knowledge and information exchange on fiscal policy in support of 
shifting greater investment in and development of common goods for health to promote 
economic, environmental and social sustainability, according to the budgetary possibilities, 
while ensuring their efficiency and fiscal sustainability; 
(OP)3. REQUESTS the Director-General: 
(1) to develop, in consultation with Member States and within available resources as 
appropriate, a strategy on how to implement an economics of health for all approach, 
including priority actions for Member States and other actors, for consideration by the 
Seventy-ninth World Health Assembly in 2026, through the Executive Board at its 158th 
session; 
(2) to develop and sustain a cross-cutting programme of work on economics and health 
for all, within existing resources as appropriate, including strategic, normative, advocacy, 
technical, analytical and engagement components, within the WHO Health Finance and

 COMMITTEE B: FOURTH MEETING 265 
 
 
 
 
The representative of SAUDI ARABIA expressed appreciation for the Secretariat’s efforts 
concerning the implementation of the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes and 
the guidance on ending the inappropriate promotion of foods for infants and young children. It was 
important to implement measures restricting the digital marketing of breast-milk substitutes and increase 
public awareness of the issue. His Government was committed to implementing the global framework 
for integrating well-being into public health utilizing a health promotion approach and to addressing the 
social determinants of health. Given the close interrelationship between economic development and 
health, he highlighted the importance of a whole-of-government approach and increased investment, 
sustainable financing and innovation for health. 
The representative of BRAZIL, speaking also on behalf of Armenia, Bangladesh, Belgium, the 
Plurinational State of Bolivia, Botswana, Colombia, the Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, 
Guatemala, Honduras, Hungary, Indonesia, Jamaica, Kenya, Mexico, Nicaragua, Panama, Peru, 
Slovakia, Slovenia, South Africa, Sri Lanka, the Syrian Arab Republic, Thailand and Uruguay, said that 
despite the scientifically proven benefits of breastfeeding, less than half of infants and young children 
worldwide were breastfed in accordance with WHO recommendations, in part owing to the powerful 
influence of marketing of breast-milk substitutes. Given that digital environments were fast becoming 
the predominant source of exposure to that marketing, he expressed support for the guidance on 
regulatory measures aimed at restricting digital marketing of breast-milk substitutes. His Government 
intended to propose a draft resolution on the matter to the Seventy-eighth World Health Assembly in 
May 2025 and would request an amendment to its agenda accordingly. 
The representative of ANGOLA, speaking on behalf of the Member States of the African Region, 
acknowledged efforts to address the social determinants of health through multisectoral action guided 
by social justice, inclusion and solidarity. The Secretariat should intensify support to Member States in 
developing innovations addressing the social, economic, environmental and cultural determinants of 
health. It was to be hoped that ministers of finance, agriculture, labour and education would participate 
in global health forums in the future.  
The Africa Regional Nutrition Strategy of the African Union and the WHO Strategic plan to 
reduce the double burden of malnutrition in the African region (2019–2025) provided frameworks for 
implementing the Comprehensive Implementation Plan on Maternal, Infant and Young Child Nutrition. 
Exclusive breastfeeding rates were increasingly threatened by digital marketing of breast-milk 
substitutes, and overweight and obesity were increasing, especially among children and adolescents. She 
called for increased support from the Secretariat and partners to address nutrition-related challenges in 
the Region, particularly in the context of climate change, and to strengthen regulatory frameworks to 
combat unethical marketing of unhealthy foods, including breast-milk substitutes. Countries in the 
Region continued to face challenges arising from inadequate health infrastructure in rural areas and 
insufficient human and financial resources. The double burden of malnutrition required a holistic, 
coordinated approach, with progress hinging on efforts to strengthen international collaboration, engage 
sectors beyond the health sector and mobilize additional resources while ensuring their effective 
utilization.  
She highlighted the fundamental relationship between health and the economy and expressed 
appreciation for efforts made by countries in implementing the global framework for integrating  
well-being into public health utilizing a health promotion approach. She supported the draft resolution 
on strengthening health and well-being through sport events. 
The representative of INDIA, speaking on behalf of the Member States of the South-East Asia 
Region, said that countries in the Region were facing significant challenges related to ageing and were 
undergoing a major digital transformation, necessitating a comprehensive approach to health. The 
Regional Strategic Framework on Social Determinants of Health Actions in South-East Asia  
(2023–2030) was guiding their response to health inequities and the economic, commercial and digital 
determinants of health. To improve health systems, collection of comprehensive, disaggregated data was 
needed. Universal health and social protection systems for vulnerable populations were recommended, 
266 SEVENTY-SEVENTH WORLD HEALTH ASSEMBLY 
 
 
 
 
as was investment in social capital, participation and governance for health and well-being, especially 
in low-resource settings. 
Countries in the Region were implementing the Comprehensive Implementation Plan for 
Maternal, Infant and Young Child Nutrition. Under-5 stunting had reduced, the Region was on track to 
reach global childhood overweight targets by 2025 and Member States were committed to scaling up 
strategies to address low birth weight and wasting. Health literacy and community engagement were 
crucial for improving access to appropriate nutrition among vulnerable groups. Preventing domestic 
violence, especially against children, was key to improving health and well-being among vulnerable 
populations, and support should be provided to early education and child learning centres so that needs 
for nutritious meals could be assessed. 
She highlighted the value of a comprehensive approach to well-being in all settings, noting the 
importance of curbing harmful products and practices and negative commercial determinants of health. 
She expressed support for the draft resolution on strengthening health and well-being through sports 
events, adding that integrating holistic and complementary traditional, evidence-based practices such as 
yoga encouraged a comprehensive approach to health.  
Addressing economic determinants that led to health inequities was particularly important for 
supporting vulnerable, marginalized and hard-to-reach populations. She called for a thorough analysis 
of the economic benefits of healthy populations and of the ways in which traditional medicines and 
wellness initiatives could contribute to national economies in the Region.  
The representative of BELGIUM, speaking on behalf of the European Union and its Member 
States, said that the candidate countries North Macedonia, Montenegro, Albania, the Republic of 
Moldova, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Georgia aligned themselves with his statement. Regarding the 
social determinants of health, he called on Member States to address underlying inequities, in particular 
the rise in poverty linked to conflicts and the triple planetary crisis. Social protection and a gender 
perspective would be key to those efforts. Effective interventions centred on individuals and their 
environments were needed to address health determinants and risk factors, which could be individual or 
collective, environmental, social or economic. 
In recent years, Member States had called for the relationship between health, well-being and the 
economy to be redefined. A sustainable economy that integrated environmental and social factors 
facilitated action to address ongoing national and global health challenges. He welcomed the call to shift 
public and private investment from activities that harmed human and planetary health towards activities 
that improved them, noting the importance of increasing equality in health outcomes. Improving 
dialogue among ministers of health, finance and the economy and other stakeholders would enhance 
public capacity and drive public-private collaboration for health. To that end, the Secretariat should 
strengthen its macroeconomic expertise to support health ministers in making the case for investing in 
health. His group welcomed the draft resolution on economics of health for all. 
The representative of JORDAN, speaking on behalf of the Member States of the Eastern 
Mediterranean Region, said that countries in the Region were implementing recommendations issued 
by the Commission on Social Determinants of Health in the Eastern Mediterranean. While progress in 
achieving the global nutrition targets had often been disrupted by emergencies and economic pressures, 
Member States in the Region were committed to addressing the double burden of malnutrition. The 
Secretariat and WHO partners should continue to prioritize maternal, infant and young child nutrition 
after the end of the Comprehensive Implementation Plan for Maternal, Infant and Young Child 
Nutrition. WHO should continue to prioritize well-being and health promotion as a core part of its 
mission, which would require sustained, coherent, long-term, multisectoral action and would often 
involve confronting powerful vested interests. International commitments and instruments would be 
essential to maintaining momentum in that regard. 
The representative of MALAYSIA, describing initiatives implemented in his country, 
emphasized the importance of a collective, whole-of-government approach to addressing the key 
structural determinants of health. Further consultation on implementing the guidance on regulatory

measures aimed at restricting digital marketing of breast-milk substitutes was needed, with a particular

at restricting digital marketing of breast-milk substitutes, supported by technical consultations with

The representative of NORWAY, speaking as her country’s youth delegate, expressed concern at 
the lack of progress in implementing the Comprehensive Implementation Plan on Maternal, Infant and 
Young Child Nutrition, which her Government supported extending to 2030 to align with the 
Sustainable Development Goals. Intensified efforts, evidence-based measures and national and 
international leadership were needed to reach its targets, and the International Code of Marketing of

The representative of GERMANY said that strengthening social protection systems was key to 
reducing health inequities. Governments should consider implementing social protection measures 
beyond income transfers, such as contributory social protection schemes, and should centre social 
protection systems around environmental strategies. Health interventions and systems were much more 
effective when a gender-responsive approach was adopted. The impact of social and commercial 
determinants must be addressed by promoting healthy behaviours.

Public bodies needed to be adequately resourced and strengthened to support well-being and

The representative of QATAR said that the objective of the draft resolution on strengthening 
health and well-being through sport events was to urge Member States, international organizations and 
non-State actors to harness the power of sport events to address public health challenges including 
noncommunicable diseases, mental health and physical inactivity. The draft resolution was aligned with 
established international agreements and highlighted the need for evidence-based health promotion 
measures and effective intersectoral collaboration. Furthermore, it underscored the importance of 
evaluating short-, medium- and long-term health impacts, encouraging global cooperation and 
enhancing access to sport and physical activity, particularly among at-risk populations. He encouraged

The representative of PARAGUAY shared information on her Government’s efforts to promote 
health and well-being, and highlighted the importance of adequate child nutrition. Economics and health

and implementing effective public policies.

of health and invest in both health and non-health interventions to accelerate progress. To that end, a 
multifaceted approach and innovative financing mechanisms were needed, alongside a renewed focus 
on social solidarity in health care funding. Health considerations should be integrated into all 
government policies, and cross-sectoral collaboration strengthened. It was also vital to empower health 
care professionals through competitive compensation, career development opportunities and positive 
work environments. WHO’s continued leadership was important in unifying donor funding for health 
programmes, regulating misleading food marketing practices and advocating for healthier food options. 
The promotion of breastfeeding, nutrition and physical activity were also key to fostering healthy 
lifestyles. Technical support should be provided in the area of strong financial management, which was 
the foundation of a robust health care system.

and young children should also continue to be explored.

promotion approach, she highlighted the importance of coordination and collaboration between health

The CHAIR said that, once all Member States and participants wishing to speak had taken the 
floor, separate votes on the draft decision and the draft resolution would be taken by roll-call, following

The representative of BELGIUM, speaking on behalf of the European Union and its Member 
States, said that the candidate countries North Macedonia, Montenegro, Albania, Ukraine and the 
Republic of Moldova aligned themselves with his statement. The rise of more frequent, complex and 
prolonged health emergencies around the world was alarming, as was the resulting global surge in 
humanitarian health needs. He condemned the illegal, unprovoked and unjustified war of aggression 
waged by the Government of the Russian Federation against Ukraine, which violated international law 
and the Charter of the United Nations. The resulting health and humanitarian crisis in Ukraine was 
significant and unwarranted. He called on the Government of the Russian Federation to immediately 
cease hostilities, including attacks on health care facilities and health workers, and to uphold 
international human rights and international humanitarian law.  
The consequences of the war were not limited to Ukraine and also exacerbated the global food 
security crisis. Additionally, the increasing risk of radiological, biological and chemical events could 
have a severe impact in the region and beyond. He encouraged the Secretariat to take further action to 
mitigate the adverse health and humanitarian impacts of the war and continue to support the Ukrainian 
health care system and workers.

The draft resolution was an attempt to absolve the Government of the Russian Federation of all 
responsibility for its aggression towards Ukraine and the ensuing health emergency. He called on all

was in clear breach of international law and the Charter of the United Nations, and had had a grave

The representative of ALGERIA, speaking in explanation of vote, wished to dissociate her 
Government from any resolution that equated victims with aggressors and from any language in the 
resolution that could be construed as legitimizing the occupation. The failure to include a reference to 
an immediate ceasefire in the resolution was deplorable. 
The representative of TUNISIA, speaking in explanation of vote, said that he had abstained from 
voting because the resolution equated victims with aggressors and did not clearly call for an immediate 
ceasefire and for the admission of humanitarian aid into occupied Palestinian territory. 
The representative of the SYRIAN ARAB REPUBLIC, speaking in explanation of vote, said that 
he had voted in favour of the resolution even though the language lacked some clarity and in spite of his 
Government’s reservations about the use of any language that might equate victims with aggressors. 
Furthermore, the extent of the Israeli occupation could have been more accurately reflected. 
The representative of the UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, speaking in explanation of vote, said 
that she had abstained from voting. She reiterated that her Government did not agree with every aspect 
of the resolution and said that the lack of balance in the resolution was regrettable, notably the failure to 
condemn the 7 October 2023 terrorist attacks and the taking of hostages. Her Government’s reservations 
about paragraph 2 remained. She clarified that the resolution applied solely to the current situation in 
the Gaza Strip; no part of the resolution should be understood to alter the current state of conventional 
or customary international law, or to create rights or obligations under international law.  
The representative of ARGENTINA, speaking in explanation of vote, said that he had voted in 
favour of the resolution. He expressed deep concern regarding the challenging health situation in the 
Gaza Strip but said that the lack of balance in the text was regrettable. He reiterated his condemnation 
of the terrorist attacks carried out by Hamas, recognized Israel’s right to self-defence and echoed the 
call for the immediate and unconditional release of the hostages. 
The representative of the KINGDOM OF THE NETHERLANDS, speaking in explanation of 
vote, commended WHO for its important work in providing much needed support to the Palestinian 
people and supported the main objective of the resolution. However, consensus had been broken. Having 
reviewed the text of the resolution, her Government had found some essential elements to be missing, 
namely a call for the release of the hostages and condemnation of the gender-based violence that had 
taken place during and after the attacks on 7 October 2023. She had therefore abstained from voting. 
The representative of SWITZERLAND, speaking in explanation of vote, supported the approval 
of the resolution, which had been adopted by the Executive Board by consensus, had been the result of 
a delicate compromise and was focused on health and WHO’s mandate. It contained important elements, 
including the call to respect international humanitarian law and to protect the civilian population. 
Consensus was a sign of unity that underscored commitment to WHO’s fundamental role of preserving 
the health of populations in emergency situations. She drew attention to the recommendations set out in 
the report. 
The representative of the ISLAMIC REPUBLIC OF IRAN, speaking in explanation of vote, said 
that he wished to disassociate his Government from paragraphs 2 and 3 of the resolution and from any 
other language in the resolution that legitimized the occupying power. 
The Observer of PALESTINE thanked the Director-General for his comments and also all 
Member States who had voted in favour of the draft resolution. He highlighted the criminal nature of 
the genocide, and said that it was regrettable that the resolution had been used as a political platform 
rather than to ensure health for all.
